title: The Call of the Void: Don’t Pick Up!
summary: Josh and Chuck (with a third speaker) examine the "call of the void," also called high place phenomenon (HPP) or lapel do, the sudden urge or intrusive thought to jump from a high place or to swerve into traffic. They cover philosophical takes from Kierkegaard (anxiety and the dizziness of freedom), Sartre (vertigo of possibility, future self's freedom), and Gary Cox (bad faith). They discuss intrusive thoughts, OCD and morbid obsessions, and exposure and response prevention therapy, plus cases where mothers lost children after disclosing intrusive thoughts. Studies covered include a 2011 Florida State study by Jennifer Hames (431 students, about 43% of non-suicidal general population reporting HPP when asked about thinking of jumping), a 2020 German study by Tobias Ticsman et al. (flight phobia and online survey samples), and theories from Paul Salkovskis, Adam Anderson, Daniel Freeman, and Emil Gabriel Bruno, plus novelist Judith Dankoff's account of Deception Pass Bridge. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about bumper jingles.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to the call of the void
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the philosophy-themed episode and define the call of the void or high place phenomenon, the urge to jump from a height, with examples from film and TV.

segments.title: Personal experiences and definition of the urge
segments.summary: Chuck explains how the urge can be an intrusive thought or an urge to move away from an edge. Josh shares personal experiences and a friend's fatal fall.

segments.title: Kierkegaard and anxiety
segments.summary: Kierkegaard argued the call of the void illustrates anxiety arising from the dizziness of freedom, the inward threat of choice rather than external danger.

segments.title: Rush lyric tangent
segments.summary: A brief tangent in which the hosts discuss a Rush lyric about choosing not to decide and a mistake on the album.

segments.title: Sartre and the vertigo of possibility
segments.summary: Sartre described a vertigo of possibility and the idea that one's future self has the same freedom to choose, making the self fluid and unstable.

segments.title: Gambling example and Gary Cox on bad faith
segments.summary: Sartre's gambler example about repeating past behavior, and Gary Cox's view that psychological defenses are illusions and the call of the void exposes bad faith.

segments.title: Intrusive thoughts, OCD and exposure therapy
segments.summary: Intrusive thoughts are defined as out-of-character unwanted thoughts; they are central to OCD, morbid obsessions, and can be self-treated or treated with exposure and response prevention. Historical misuse of psychiatric interpretations led to child custody losses for mothers who disclosed such thoughts.

segments.title: Florida State study by Jennifer Hames
segments.summary: A 2011 study of 431 FSU students found over 30 percent had felt the urge to jump; about 17 percent of non-suicidal students had felt it, and reframing the question raised general-population rates to about 43 percent. Freud's death drive explanation was rejected.

segments.title: Anxiety link and survival instinct explanation
segments.summary: Hames and colleagues linked HPP to anxiety, suggesting anxious people notice internal signals more. They also framed the urge as reflecting a survival instinct.

segments.title: Ticsman 2020 German study on flight phobia and acrophobia
segments.summary: A 2020 study by Tobias Ticsman and colleagues at Ruhr University Bochum surveyed 276 online participants and 94 flight phobia patients; HPP rates matched the general population in acrophobia patients, suggesting it does not stem from fear of heights.

segments.title: Break and transition
segments.summary: Short break and transition to the next speculative theories section.

segments.title: Theories from Salkovskis, Anderson, Freeman and Bruno
segments.summary: Paul Salkovskis proposed the urge is a problem-solving thought the rational brain rejects. Adam Anderson at Cornell argued the lizard brain seeks ground safety. Daniel Freeman of Oxford considered it part of acrophobia. Emil Gabriel Bruno's work on frontal cortex damage was mentioned as a case where people may act on the urge.

segments.title: Judith Dankoff and Deception Pass Bridge
segments.summary: Novelist Judith Dankoff described an urge to jump from Deception Pass Bridge in Washington State, so strong she sat down in the middle of the bridge.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts summarize that the call of the void is common and not fully explained, and move to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: bumper jingles
segments.summary: A listener named Rob asks for a collection of the show's bumper jingles, which are made by listeners, usually under twelve seconds. Hosts invite more submissions.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and contact information for submissions.
